Adoption Crisis KZN

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
With over 1.2 million children in need of adoption, why is our adoption rate declining to 1500 a year and why did KZN province only grant eight adoptions in 2016? CB investigates

Unique Selling Point:
Hundreds of thousands of South Africans are in effect 'adopting' children annually, but that doesn't reflect in our official adoption figures, and we are still facing an adoption crisis country wide. Are South Africa's orphans without any family the real losers? Carte Blanche investigates

Summary:
There are an estimated 3 million orphaned and abandoned children in South Africa with 1,2 million of them in potential need of adoption, of which at least 3 500 are abandoned babies. The country’s adoption rate has declined in recent years from an annual rate of 2500 adoptions to a mere 1600 begging the question, what happens to the rest of the these vulnerable members of society that are need of a loving family.

In May 2016 the Department of social Development in the KZN brought a relative halt to adoptions in the province, sighting an unfounded threat of Child trafficking. As a result only 8 adoptions took place in 2016 whilst a host of them were put on ice and hamstrung by bureaucracy in a province estimated to have the highest number of orphans.

Cultural perceptions have been cited by roll players, as one of the major reasons why adoptions have slowed down in the country. The majority of children being adopted are black, whilst the majority of adoptive parents are white, however there are cases where same race adoptions have also been frowned upon as in the case of Bonnie and Michael, who have been virtually coerced into fostering by the DSD in KZN, making this a complex issue. Do these intrinsic undertones form part of the KZN's DSD rationale when approaching adoptions? Carte Blanche investigates

Further information:
Social workers and adoption lobbyists in KZN, report that the department of social development in KZN is in favour of extended family searches that are deemed unnecessary beyond the 60-day period that the child act affords them, even going as far as violating the rights of young mother's giving up their children for adoption without wanting any family to know, by searching and approaching the family of the birth mother. Child fostering is also encouraged and appears to be preferred above adoption by the DSD in KZN, instead of speedily trying to place children with matched parents. This has resulted in children staying in homes a lot longer than they should, depriving them of essential primary care bonding during their developmental years. Ultimately they are becoming the casualties of a system on a “go slow”.

There appears to be a schism between the legal backdrop and the mind set of the DSD when dealing with adoptions.

Black South Africans take on vulnerable family members and relatives daily in the form of informal adoptions and within African culture the concept of adoption is anathema and counter cultural. Orphaned children are automatically taken on by family members, looked after and assimilated into their current family situation. This falls in harmony with traditional thinking in terms of retaining one's ancestry at all costs. Therefore it is less likely for a black South African family to seek to adopt formally, although it is on the increase.

Marietjie Strydom a social worker and Head of the National Adoption Coalition (NACSA) in KZN, says research shows that a prolonged stay in an Institutionalized environment can be detrimental to the development a child, especially during their first 1000 days, and tend to suffer from attachment issues without a primary care giver. However this is becoming the fate of many children who are in the process of being adopted, or who still need to be made adoptable. This process can be lengthy as the children's families need to be traced and given the first option as to whether they are willing to take care of the orphaned child. Marietjie says, the DSD's apparent slow down is impacting detrimentally on these children's long term well-being. According to the WHO, 11% of children world wide suffer from learning disabilities, but it increases up to 30% for children who have spent their lives in homes without a primary care giver.

The problem is even more evident in South Africa when we have over 3500 abandoned children annually, who have no hope of their families ever being traced or to be placed with any form of kin. This number far exceeds the rate of adoption placements. Some children's homes like Justin Foxton's, find themselves breaking the law, as they are only accredited to keep 6 babies at a time, but there aren't enough homes so they are often taking on more children than is permitted. The question remains if there are parents wanting to adopt babies, why are they not being placed timeously ?

Justin Foxton, is a seasoned child protection activist and an adoptive parent himself, he says the slow rate of adoptions in KZN has impacted heavily on, not only his baby home, but the children as well. In a home where they used to complete 12 adoptions a year, they haven’t managed to conclude 1 in over 18 months. Justin believes that the heart of the problem may lie in the difference of our cultural beliefs. He says his journey and perceptions as a white parent to a black child have changed dramatically over the years. He is starting to speak about the decolonization of adoption and that a proper dialogue needs to be opened up with the DSD on reaching a middle ground and perhaps finding a more culturally inclusive approach to adoption that is still within the bounds of the law and can ultimately benefit those that need it most – the unwanted children of our society.

To paint a broader picture of the crisis, Julie Todd, from Pietermaritzburg Child welfare has worked for years as a social worker dealing with various cases of child adoptions in the province. She has worked on cases were she believes the department of social services in KZN have acted unlawfully by delaying adoption processes. They have even gone as far as questioning the reasons why a mother would give consent to give away her child, which is illegal and against the child act. The child Act states, that once a mother has given consent with the court it cannot be questioned. (Please note she wants her identity hidden fearing antagonizing herself with the DSD)

Bonnie and Micheal are black South Africans who were desperate to have a child of their own. They both work in a domestic environment. They decided on the adoption route and approached the KZN DSD for a same race adoption.  But instead of matching the family with a baby as they requested, they matched them to a 5 year old girl who had been removed from her mother because she was in danger. They were uncertain about the match because of the child’s age, but were told that it was their only option.  They ended up waiting over a year for their child to be placed with them. 

During this time, she was living in a CYCC despite having willing adoptive parents.  When she was finally placed with the couple in December 2016, they were informed that they would have to foster her for two years before they could formally adopt her. But her they cannot understand why they are not yet able to adopt her and why she remained in a CYCC for so long when she could have been living with her new parents. In addition, the birth mother happens to come from the same village as them, so this may cause a problem when they do go home with her. The department's attitude to this adoption is perplexing and we will take them to task. (Bonnie and Michael are willing to speak on camera but want just their names to be changed.)

In the case of Nikki and Stephen we are looking at an inter country adoption as well as a trans race adoption. These are particularly hard if not almost impossible to get passed.

Stephen and Nikki are based in the UK, but Nikki is a South African so they had to go through an international adoption process. They started their process in 2013 with initial preparation. They began the adoption process in March 2014 and were approved in the UK and their file was forwarded to Child Welfare in Durban (CWDD) to be matched to a child.  Their son Smanga was born prematurely in January 2015 and had been abandoned at birth. 

Their journey has been a hard one as they’ve had their approval rescinded at one point. Their case was stalled until they and another two couples decided to take the department to court, where the court over ruled and granted them the adoption order despite the department's resistance. In this instance there was very little reason apart from it being an inter country adoption not to grant the adoption order, but the department simply stalled, leaving little Smanga without his new parents. They are passionate about telling their story and want to help prospective adoptive parents. They hope their story will make a difference.

Ms Nokuthula Khanyile, the HOD at the department of social Development in the province denies that the department isn't acting in the best interest of the child. According to her everything is running smoothly in the province regarding adoptions apart from a few complaints she has received regarding the lengthy, thorough and detailed process of adoption that was approved by the courts. Ms khanyile disagrees with the sentiments that her department is deliberately stalling on adoptions leaving vulnerable children stranded in CYCCs.

We will take her to task on this, but also broach the cultural issue and ask what the department's protocol is exactly when it comes to processing adoptions.

Tebogo Mabe from the National department of social department speaks to the crisis on a national scale. Why has there been an overall decline in the country with adoptions slowing down? Mr Mabe’s portfolio deals directly with adoptions. He underlines for us the procedural and moral approach to adoptions for the DSD and outlines the plans with regard to the children stuck in CCYCs as processes take longer.

Nonboniso Gasa is a researcher and analyst on cultural issues and he will speak about the African concept of adoption and the role ancestry plays. He will open up the discussion as to why the department and the country as a whole may be resistant to the concept as opposed to fostering which seems the preferred route, and how this fits into the cultural mind set.

Extra Budget Items:
Travel to Durban, 2 day shoot, and film in Johannesburg with the DSD = 3 day shoot.

Press Release:


From around 2500 children adopted annually to just 1200. The rate of child adoptions in South Africa is declining. Extended family searches and delays in approving adoptions by the department of social development in KZN resulted in only 8 adoptions in 2016. It's the African way to take care of a family member who is need of a home, but for many children that are abandoned, without adoption institutional care may be their only fate.

Script:


VO: Makhosi is a five year old orphan growing up in a children's home. She is one of millions of South Africa's children who's stories are steeped in tragedy. One day she hopes to be with a family of her own.

Claire: How many successful adoptions have you had?

Asnith: one ...
Claire: And that one you said the department wasn't helpful?

VO: For 17 years Asnith Teffo has run an Early Child Development Centre in Midrand. Some of the children in her care are now matriculating, having spent most of their lives at this home.

Aznith: when we started it was a place of safety, kids weren't supposed to be here for more than six months some of the kids were forgotten by the social workers. When you phone to ask if you're remembering that the kids are still here they would say they don't remember them.

LInk: There are an estimated 3 million orphaned or abandoned children in South Africa with at least 1.2 million of them in potential need of adoption.

VO: Nationally, adoption figures have dropped substantially over the years from 2500 annually to 1165 in 2016, and in KZN the province with the most orphaned and abandoned children, there have only been 174 adoptions in the last 6 years. Robyn Wolfson Vorster, a child protection advocate believes there is an adoption crisis.

Robyn: The fact that those numbers are so low is extremely problematic and they can only be low, because those children are being cared for in impermanent relationships.

VO: Busi and Siya were desperate to have a child of their own. Two years ago they approached the Department of Social Development in Kwa Zulu Natal. They wanted to adopt a baby but the social worker presented them with a 4 year old girl.

Bonnie: So we welcomed her even though she wasn't what we were hoping for, but we were happy to have found her there.

Robyn: We know in SA we have a lot of children in need of adoption. There would be no reason to place an older child with a family who have specifically asked for a baby.

VO: Robyn believes the Department acted unethically and should have disclosed to the couple that it was not accredited to process adoptions at the time.

Claire: Did that social worker tell you that the child was ready for adoption?
Bonnie: she said we must foster her first and after two years we can take her as our own child.

VO: So after a year and a half of infrequent visits Busi and Siya were able to bring their child home, and only then were they informed of the child's background.

Bonnie: So when the social worker found her, her mother was holding her by her leg. She was drunk.

VO: They also told them the child's abusive mother came from the same town, and they would need to get her written consent. The social worker did not explain that fostering may be impermanent.

Siya: the social worker said they want to find the family first.
Bonnie: That is why we fear that they might still take the child away.

VO: Many social workers feel the Department of Social Development in the province does not encourage adoption and will go to any lengths to reunite families first, says Marietjie Strydom,of the National adoption coalition.

Marietjie: the department of social development acting according to the law will say family reunification is the outmost priority There might be a variety of contributing factors, it might be substance misuse, it might be mental health difficulties. These are the complexities that need to be talked about if we are going to act in the best interest of the child.

VO: We met with Nokuthula Kanyile, HOD of the Department of Social Development in KZN and presented the circumstances of the case to her.

Nokuthula: I would love to hear from the social worker first what happened because they would normally know where the child's family of origin is before making permanent decisions. I don't think they communicated to the social worker explicitly what they wanted to do.

VO: Busi and Siya's story is not an isolated one.
Families report they are afraid to speak out, for fear of losing their foster children and that these attitudes by the department, dissuade them from applying for adoption.

Robyn: If you look at their annual reports they have a very high priority on family preservation and family reunification. They also have key performance indicators on how many children they place in foster care. In the last two years they placed 64000 children. However there is no performance indicator for adoption.

Nokuthula: Yes we are preferring reunification. Families is the most primary unit to bring up a child.

Link: In african tradition blood relation and ancestral ties are paramount to our belief system. it is believed that out of family child adoptions are a foreign practice

VO: Professor Sihawukele Ngubane heads up cultural studies at the University of Kwa Zulu Natal

Professor Ngubane: Among Africans parenting it is a collective, so we have a different point of view between Western and African we believe the children come from our ancestors. Non kin adoption is a problem, what is acceptable is a kinship adoption because they share the same blood relative.

VO: Traditionally African culture integrates orphans into community and family and legalised adoption is not common practice. The generally low take up of formalised adoptions was compounded when

Link: in may 2016 the department of social development in KZN put out a memorandum that stopped child adoptions in the province

VO: Justin Foxton who runs a baby home in KZN says they have processed zero adoptions since then.

Justin: Children were being literally left, their cases not moving forward at any great pace even if they were adoptable.

VO: We showed the HOD this memorandum, and asked why there was ostensibly a moratorium placed on adoptions for six months in 2016

Nokuthula: This is not a moratorium and this is an internal communication of the department talking about the withdrawal of delegation. We never stopped adoptions

VO: But a withdrawal of delegation means that no adoptions took place as no panel sessions were held. Marietjie Strydom says the reason the department gave, was linked to suspicions of child trafficking.

Marietjie: There were allegations made that a family who had already adopted would have gone on to then have their children adopted internationally.

Robyn: The family that were accused of child trafficking, they sent me an email to say the department continues to pursue them but they have however been cleared by the hawks and the child protection unit

VO: When Nikki and Stephen Mepham, applied for their inter-country adoption they inadvertently found themselves caught in this stalemate. Now living in the UK they had met as young doctors doing community service in rural KZN. //After undergoing a rigorous screening process they were matched to a baby, Smangaliso from Kwa Zulu Natal.

Nikki: His family had not been found, he was abandoned at birth. All that stood in our way from coming to South Africa to proceed with the adoption was the 239D letter required by the KZN DSD.

Link: The department of social development is responsible for the 239D letter which effectively permits a successful adoption. For social workers and adoptive parents this has been the biggest hurdle in KZN

VO: Months went by and repeated postponements, for approval of the 239D letter, led the Mepham's to take their case to the South African high court, because their adoption continued to be opposed by the department

Nikki: Why they would not consent was that they wanted to attempt family reunification despite the fact that that had already been attempted


Nokuthula: We have done a diagnosis of our own internal weaknesses and we have identified that the people who were signing the section 239 letters were not doing a proper interrogation and quality assurance.

VO: The result of this extreme scrutiny was that only eight adoptions were granted in the province in 2016, according to this department document presented to Social workers late last year But the HOD flatly denied that this was the case and insisted on referring to a different time frame.

Nokuthula: When we look at reviewing our performance for the past 12 months. That is from September 2016 to date, 40 of the 53 applications for adoption have been successful and recommended to court and that marks almost to 75% of the cases that have been finalized.

Claire: Are you saying that only 53 people requested or put through submissions to adopt in the province?

Nokuthula: Yes adoptions are not in high demand

VO: These 40 adoptions only addressed the period from November 2016 to date and despite the HOD’s assertions, when the department sent official figures to Carte Blanche days after the interview, they confirmed that only 8 adoptions were recorded before November 2016.

Robyn: The department say that 75% of their cases have been processed, they're possibly not talking about all the others that are in backlog.

VO: On request from Carte Blanche, Social workers in KZN compiled statistics from their records from November 2016 to date. According to them there were 129 applications for adoption as opposed to the departments 53.
Only a 30% success rate as opposed to the departments 75%

On average it's taking the department 6 months to finalise an adoption.

Both the social workers and the department's figures confirm the smallest number of adoptions granted in the province are cross-cultural.

Nokuthula: Once you send the child outside the culture by law, the primary placement is for compatibility in terms of cultural background.

VO: Although cultural identity is critical, there are children who could benefit from adoption and Nikki and Stephen fought their battle in a court of law. In the High Court the Head of Department finally conceded that a 239 letter is not required for inter-country adoptions. This set a legal precedent for future inter-country adoptions, and after seven months of waiting, Smanga could finally have a family of his own.

Nikki: Those 7 months were a time where Smanga could have been with a family. A critical time of his development, part of the first 1000 days and he will never get that back.

Aznith: A home has its own challenges. its a group of children living under the same roof and that element of quality rearing of a child from a mom and dad isnt there.

Justin: A simple moratorium for whatever practical reasons that is implemented is going to hamper a childs life for the rest of its life.

VO: But the HOD's approach to adoption in KZN is clear

Nokuthula: From where I sit there is no crisis
you'll see that adoption is not in demand compared to other forms of alternative placements for children.

VO: But if adoption is not even presented to prospective parents like Busi and Siya despite their wishes, their new found family will now be filled with uncertainty and they may lose the child they have grown to love

FIN!!!!!
ENDS!!!!!!!

Nokuthula: Adoptions are not in high demand


PROMO 15”

Their son Smanga was born prematurely in January 2015 and had been abandoned at birth. Their journey has been a hard one as they’ve had their approval rescinded at one point. Their case was stalled until they and another two couples decided to take the department to court, where the court over ruled and granted them the adoption order despite the department's resistance. In this instance there was very little reason apart from it being an inter country adoption not to grant the adoption order, but the department simply stalled, leaving little Smanga without his new parents. They are passionate about telling their story and want to help prospective adoptive parents. They hope their story will make a difference. Ms Nokuthula Khanyile, the HOD at the department of social Development in the province denies that the department isn't acting in the best interest of the child. According to her everything is running smoothly in the province regarding adoptions apart from a few complaints she has received regarding the lengthy, thorough and detailed process of adoption that was approved by the courts. Ms khanyile disagrees with the sentiments that her department is deliberately stalling on adoptions leaving vulnerable children stranded in CYCCs. We will take her to task on this, but also broach the cultural issue and ask what the department's protocol is exactly when it comes to processing adoptions. Tebogo Mabe from the National department of social department speaks to the crisis on a national scale. Why has there been an overall decline in the country with adoptions slowing down? Mr Mabe’s portfolio deals directly with adoptions. He underlines for us the procedural and moral approach to adoptions for the DSD and outlines the plans with regard to the children stuck in CCYCs as processes take longer. Nonboniso Gasa is a researcher and analyst on cultural issues and he will speak about the African concept of adoption and the role ancestry plays. He will open up the discussion as to why the department and the country as a whole may be resistant to the concept as opposed to fostering which seems the preferred route, and how this fits into the cultural mind set. Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 06 December 2017 03 September 2017 - Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 28 September 2017 Press Release: From around 2500 children adopted annually to just 1200. The rate of child adoptions in South Africa is declining. Extended family searches and delays in approving adoptions by the department of social development in KZN resulted in only 8 adoptions in 2016. It's the African way to take care of a family member who is need of a home, but for many children that are abandoned, without adoption institutional care may be their only fate. Script: VO: Makhosi is a five year old orphan growing up in a children's home. She is one of millions of South Africa's children who's stories are steeped in tragedy. One day she hopes to be with a family of her own. Claire: How many successful adoptions have you had? Asnith: one ... Claire: And that one you said the department wasn't helpful? VO: For 17 years Asnith Teffo has run an Early Child Development Centre in Midrand. Some of the children in her care are now matriculating, having spent most of their lives at this home. Aznith: when we started it was a place of safety, kids weren't supposed to be here for more than six months some of the kids were forgotten by the social workers. When you phone to ask if you're remembering that the kids are still here they would say they don't remember them. LInk: There are an estimated 3 million orphaned or abandoned children in South Africa with at least 1.2 million of them in potential need of adoption. VO: Nationally, adoption figures have dropped substantially over the years from 2500 annually to 1165 in 2016, and in KZN the province with the most orphaned and abandoned children, there have only been 174 adoptions in the last 6 years. Robyn Wolfson Vorster, a child protection advocate believes there is an adoption crisis. Robyn: The fact that those numbers are so low is extremely problematic and they can only be low, because those children are being cared for in impermanent relationships. VO: Busi and Siya were desperate to have a child of their own. Two years ago they approached the Department of Social Development in Kwa Zulu Natal. They wanted to adopt a baby but the social worker presented them with a 4 year old girl. Bonnie: So we welcomed her even though she wasn't what we were hoping for, but we were happy to have found her there. Robyn: We know in SA we have a lot of children in need of adoption. There would be no reason to place an older child with a family who have specifically asked for a baby. VO: Robyn believes the Department acted unethically and should have disclosed to the couple that it was not accredited to process adoptions at the time. Claire: Did that social worker tell you that the child was ready for adoption? Bonnie: she said we must foster her first and after two years we can take her as our own child. VO: So after a year and a half of infrequent visits Busi and Siya were able to bring their child home, and only then were they informed of the child's background. Bonnie: So when the social worker found her, her mother was holding her by her leg. She was drunk. VO: They also told them the child's abusive mother came from the same town, and they would need to get her written consent. The social worker did not explain that fostering may be impermanent. Siya: the social worker said they want to find the family first. Bonnie: That is why we fear that they might still take the child away. VO: Many social workers feel the Department of Social Development in the province does not encourage adoption and will go to any lengths to reunite families first, says Marietjie Strydom,of the National adoption coalition. Marietjie: the department of social development acting according to the law will say family reunification is the outmost priority There might be a variety of contributing factors, it might be substance misuse, it might be mental health difficulties. These are the complexities that need to be talked about if we are going to act in the best interest of the child. VO: We met with Nokuthula Kanyile, HOD of the Department of Social Development in KZN and presented the circumstances of the case to her. Nokuthula: I would love to hear from the social worker first what happened because they would normally know where the child's family of origin is before making permanent decisions. I don't think they communicated to the social worker explicitly what they wanted to do. VO: Busi and Siya's story is not an isolated one. Families report they are afraid to speak out, for fear of losing their foster children and that these attitudes by the department, dissuade them from applying for adoption. Robyn: If you look at their annual reports they have a very high priority on family preservation and family reunification. They also have key performance indicators on how many children they place in foster care. In the last two years they placed 64000 children. However there is no performance indicator for adoption. Nokuthula: Yes we are preferring reunification. Families is the most primary unit to bring up a child. Link: In african tradition blood relation and ancestral ties are paramount to our belief system. it is believed that out of family child adoptions are a foreign practice VO: Professor Sihawukele Ngubane heads up cultural studies at the University of Kwa Zulu Natal Professor Ngubane: Among Africans parenting it is a collective, so we have a different point of view between Western and African we believe the children come from our ancestors. Non kin adoption is a problem, what is acceptable is a kinship adoption because they share the same blood relative. VO: Traditionally African culture integrates orphans into community and family and legalised adoption is not common practice. The generally low take up of formalised adoptions was compounded when Link: in may 2016 the department of social development in KZN put out a memorandum that stopped child adoptions in the province VO: Justin Foxton who runs a baby home in KZN says they have processed zero adoptions since then. Justin: Children were being literally left, their cases not moving forward at any great pace even if they were adoptable. VO: We showed the HOD this memorandum, and asked why there was ostensibly a moratorium placed on adoptions for six months in 2016 Nokuthula: This is not a moratorium and this is an internal communication of the department talking about the withdrawal of delegation. We never stopped adoptions VO: But a withdrawal of delegation means that no adoptions took place as no panel sessions were held. Marietjie Strydom says the reason the department gave, was linked to suspicions of child trafficking. Marietjie: There were allegations made that a family who had already adopted would have gone on to then have their children adopted internationally. Robyn: The family that were accused of child trafficking, they sent me an email to say the department continues to pursue them but they have however been cleared by the hawks and the child protection unit VO: When Nikki and Stephen Mepham, applied for their inter-country adoption they inadvertently found themselves caught in this stalemate. Now living in the UK they had met as young doctors doing community service in rural KZN. //After undergoing a rigorous screening process they were matched to a baby, Smangaliso from Kwa Zulu Natal. Nikki: His family had not been found, he was abandoned at birth. All that stood in our way from coming to South Africa to proceed with the adoption was the 239D letter required by the KZN DSD. Link: The department of social development is responsible for the 239D letter which effectively permits a successful adoption. For social workers and adoptive parents this has been the biggest hurdle in KZN VO: Months went by and repeated postponements, for approval of the 239D letter, led the Mepham's to take their case to the South African high court, because their adoption continued to be opposed by the department Nikki: Why they would not consent was that they wanted to attempt family reunification despite the fact that that had already been attempted Nokuthula: We have done a diagnosis of our own internal weaknesses and we have identified that the people who were signing the section 239 letters were not doing a proper interrogation and quality assurance. VO: The result of this extreme scrutiny was that only eight adoptions were granted in the province in 2016, according to this department document presented to Social workers late last year But the HOD flatly denied that this was the case and insisted on referring to a different time frame. Nokuthula: When we look at reviewing our performance for the past 12 months. That is from September 2016 to date, 40 of the 53 applications for adoption have been successful and recommended to court and that marks almost to 75% of the cases that have been finalized. Claire: Are you saying that only 53 people requested or put through submissions to adopt in the province? Nokuthula: Yes adoptions are not in high demand VO: These 40 adoptions only addressed the period from November 2016 to date and despite the HOD’s assertions, when the department sent official figures to Carte Blanche days after the interview, they confirmed that only 8 adoptions were recorded before November 2016. Robyn: The department say that 75% of their cases have been processed, they're possibly not talking about all the others that are in backlog. VO: On request from Carte Blanche, Social workers in KZN compiled statistics from their records from November 2016 to date. According to them there were 129 applications for adoption as opposed to the departments 53. Only a 30% success rate as opposed to the departments 75% On average it's taking the department 6 months to finalise an adoption. Both the social workers and the department's figures confirm the smallest number of adoptions granted in the province are cross-cultural. Nokuthula: Once you send the child outside the culture by law, the primary placement is for compatibility in terms of cultural background. VO: Although cultural identity is critical, there are children who could benefit from adoption and Nikki and Stephen fought their battle in a court of law. In the High Court the Head of Department finally conceded that a 239 letter is not required for inter-country adoptions. This set a legal precedent for future inter-country adoptions, and after seven months of waiting, Smanga could finally have a family of his own. Nikki: Those 7 months were a time where Smanga could have been with a family. A critical time of his development, part of the first 1000 days and he will never get that back. Aznith: A home has its own challenges. its a group of children living under the same roof and that element of quality rearing of a child from a mom and dad isnt there. Justin: A simple moratorium for whatever practical reasons that is implemented is going to hamper a childs life for the rest of its life. VO: But the HOD's approach to adoption in KZN is clear Nokuthula: From where I sit there is no crisis you'll see that adoption is not in demand compared to other forms of alternative placements for children. VO: But if adoption is not even presented to prospective parents like Busi and Siya despite their wishes, their new found family will now be filled with uncertainty and they may lose the child they have grown to love FIN!!!!! ENDS!!!!!!! PROMOS PROMO 15” VO: With an estimated 3500 abandoned children in South Africa, and only 1200 adoptions in the past year, thousands of vulnerable children are left to grow up in institutional care. Nokuthula: Adoptions are not in high demand PROMO 15” VO: Extended family searches and delays in approving adoptions by the department of social development in KZN resulted in only 8 adoptions in 2016. Justin: Children were being literally left, their cases not moving forward at any great pace even if they were adoptable. PROMO 10” Claire Link 05: There are millions of children left orphaned and abandoned in South Africa and with the severe decline with the rate of adoptions in the country, what does the future look like for these children? PROMO 10” VO: It's the African way to take care of a family member who is need of a home, but for many children that are abandoned, without adoption institutional care may be their only fate.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): With over 1.2 million children in need of adoption, why is our adoption rate declining to 1500 a year and why did KZN province only grant eight adoptions in 2016? CB investigates
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Hundreds of thousands of South Africans are in effect 'adopting' children annually, but that doesn't reflect in our official adoption figures, and we are still facing an adoption crisis country wide. Are South Africa's orphans without any family the real losers? Carte Blanche investigates
metadata.Summary: There are an estimated 3 million orphaned and abandoned children in South Africa with 1,2 million of them in potential need of adoption, of which at least 3 500 are abandoned babies. The country’s adoption rate has declined in recent years from an annual rate of 2500 adoptions to a mere 1600 begging the question, what happens to the rest of the these vulnerable members of society that are need of a loving family. In May 2016 the Department of social Development in the KZN brought a relative halt to adoptions in the province, sighting an unfounded threat of Child trafficking. As a result only 8 adoptions took place in 2016 whilst a host of them were put on ice and hamstrung by bureaucracy in a province estimated to have the highest number of orphans. Cultural perceptions have been cited by roll players, as one of the major reasons why adoptions have slowed down in the country. The majority of children being adopted are black, whilst the majority of adoptive parents are white, however there are cases where same race adoptions have also been frowned upon as in the case of Bonnie and Michael, who have been virtually coerced into fostering by the DSD in KZN, making this a complex issue. Do these intrinsic undertones form part of the KZN's DSD rationale when approaching adoptions? Carte Blanche investigates
metadata.Further information: Social workers and adoption lobbyists in KZN, report that the department of social development in KZN is in favour of extended family searches that are deemed unnecessary beyond the 60-day period that the child act affords them, even going as far as violating the rights of young mother's giving up their children for adoption without wanting any family to know, by searching and approaching the family of the birth mother. Child fostering is also encouraged and appears to be preferred above adoption by the DSD in KZN, instead of speedily trying to place children with matched parents. This has resulted in children staying in homes a lot longer than they should, depriving them of essential primary care bonding during their developmental years. Ultimately they are becoming the casualties of a system on a “go slow”. There appears to be a schism between the legal backdrop and the mind set of the DSD when dealing with adoptions. Black South Africans take on vulnerable family members and relatives daily in the form of informal adoptions and within African culture the concept of adoption is anathema and counter cultural. Orphaned children are automatically taken on by family members, looked after and assimilated into their current family situation. This falls in harmony with traditional thinking in terms of retaining one's ancestry at all costs. Therefore it is less likely for a black South African family to seek to adopt formally, although it is on the increase. Marietjie Strydom a social worker and Head of the National Adoption Coalition (NACSA) in KZN, says research shows that a prolonged stay in an Institutionalized environment can be detrimental to the development a child, especially during their first 1000 days, and tend to suffer from attachment issues without a primary care giver. However this is becoming the fate of many children who are in the process of being adopted, or who still need to be made adoptable. This process can be lengthy as the children's families need to be traced and given the first option as to whether they are willing to take care of the orphaned child. Marietjie says, the DSD's apparent slow down is impacting detrimentally on these children's long term well-being. According to the WHO, 11% of children world wide suffer from learning disabilities, but it increases up to 30% for children who have spent their lives in homes without a primary care giver. The problem is even more evident in South Africa when we have over 3500 abandoned children annually, who have no hope of their families ever being traced or to be placed with any form of kin. This number far exceeds the rate of adoption placements. Some children's homes like Justin Foxton's, find themselves breaking the law, as they are only accredited to keep 6 babies at a time, but there aren't enough homes so they are often taking on more children than is permitted. The question remains if there are parents wanting to adopt babies, why are they not being placed timeously ? Justin Foxton, is a seasoned child protection activist and an adoptive parent himself, he says the slow rate of adoptions in KZN has impacted heavily on, not only his baby home, but the children as well. In a home where they used to complete 12 adoptions a year, they haven’t managed to conclude 1 in over 18 months. Justin believes that the heart of the problem may lie in the difference of our cultural beliefs. He says his journey and perceptions as a white parent to a black child have changed dramatically over the years. He is starting to speak about the decolonization of adoption and that a proper dialogue needs to be opened up with the DSD on reaching a middle ground and perhaps finding a more culturally inclusive approach to adoption that is still within the bounds of the law and can ultimately benefit those that need it most – the unwanted children of our society. To paint a broader picture of the crisis, Julie Todd, from Pietermaritzburg Child welfare has worked for years as a social worker dealing with various cases of child adoptions in the province. She has worked on cases were she believes the department of social services in KZN have acted unlawfully by delaying adoption processes. They have even gone as far as questioning the reasons why a mother would give consent to give away her child, which is illegal and against the child act. The child Act states, that once a mother has given consent with the court it cannot be questioned. (Please note she wants her identity hidden fearing antagonizing herself with the DSD) Bonnie and Micheal are black South Africans who were desperate to have a child of their own. They both work in a domestic environment. They decided on the adoption route and approached the KZN DSD for a same race adoption. But instead of matching the family with a baby as they requested, they matched them to a 5 year old girl who had been removed from her mother because she was in danger. They were uncertain about the match because of the child’s age, but were told that it was their only option. They ended up waiting over a year for their child to be placed with them. During this time, she was living in a CYCC despite having willing adoptive parents. When she was finally placed with the couple in December 2016, they were informed that they would have to foster her for two years before they could formally adopt her. But her they cannot understand why they are not yet able to adopt her and why she remained in a CYCC for so long when she could have been living with her new parents. In addition, the birth mother happens to come from the same village as them, so this may cause a problem when they do go home with her. The department's attitude to this adoption is perplexing and we will take them to task. (Bonnie and Michael are willing to speak on camera but want just their names to be changed.) In the case of Nikki and Stephen we are looking at an inter country adoption as well as a trans race adoption. These are particularly hard if not almost impossible to get passed. Stephen and Nikki are based in the UK, but Nikki is a South African so they had to go through an international adoption process. They started their process in 2013 with initial preparation. They began the adoption process in March 2014 and were approved in the UK and their file was forwarded to Child Welfare in Durban (CWDD) to be matched to a child. Their son Smanga was born prematurely in January 2015 and had been abandoned at birth. Their journey has been a hard one as they’ve had their approval rescinded at one point. Their case was stalled until they and another two couples decided to take the department to court, where the court over ruled and granted them the adoption order despite the department's resistance. In this instance there was very little reason apart from it being an inter country adoption not to grant the adoption order, but the department simply stalled, leaving little Smanga without his new parents. They are passionate about telling their story and want to help prospective adoptive parents. They hope their story will make a difference. Ms Nokuthula Khanyile, the HOD at the department of social Development in the province denies that the department isn't acting in the best interest of the child. According to her everything is running smoothly in the province regarding adoptions apart from a few complaints she has received regarding the lengthy, thorough and detailed process of adoption that was approved by the courts. Ms khanyile disagrees with the sentiments that her department is deliberately stalling on adoptions leaving vulnerable children stranded in CYCCs. We will take her to task on this, but also broach the cultural issue and ask what the department's protocol is exactly when it comes to processing adoptions. Tebogo Mabe from the National department of social department speaks to the crisis on a national scale. Why has there been an overall decline in the country with adoptions slowing down? Mr Mabe’s portfolio deals directly with adoptions. He underlines for us the procedural and moral approach to adoptions for the DSD and outlines the plans with regard to the children stuck in CCYCs as processes take longer. Nonboniso Gasa is a researcher and analyst on cultural issues and he will speak about the African concept of adoption and the role ancestry plays. He will open up the discussion as to why the department and the country as a whole may be resistant to the concept as opposed to fostering which seems the preferred route, and how this fits into the cultural mind set.
